title: Bachelorette Hangover Kit: What to Pack (Plus a Bachelor Version)
excerpt: What actually belongs in a bachelorette hangover kit, how to build per-person bags vs a shared recovery station, a bachelor party version, and the safety basics for a party weekend.
metaDescription: What to pack in a bachelorette hangover kit: water, electrolytes, snacks, sleep gear, and labeled painkillers. Plus a bachelor party kit and safety tips.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**What actually goes in a bachelorette hangover kit:** a refillable water bottle, a few electrolyte packets, a salty snack, a gentle breakfast item, ginger chews or mints, lip balm, a sleep mask and earplugs, and a clearly labeled single-serve painkiller with a note about alcohol. That covers the real problems of a party weekend: dehydration, an unsettled stomach, bad sleep in a shared room, and a morning headache. Supplements like DHM (dihydromyricetin) are optional extras, not the foundation. The same list works for a bachelor party with a few swaps, which we cover below.

The thing that makes a bachelorette kit different from an ordinary hangover kit is the format. It's not one bad morning, it's two or three in a row, shared by a group of people with different bodies, different medications, and different ideas of a good time. So the best kits are planned around the weekend's schedule, not just stuffed into a cute bag. This guide covers what to pack, what to leave out, how to build per-person bags versus a shared "recovery station," how to adapt it for a bachelor party, and the safety basics that every maid of honor or best man should know before the first toast.

> **This is not medical advice.** A hangover kit makes a rough morning more comfortable. It doesn't make heavy drinking safe, and nothing in it treats alcohol poisoning. **Call 911 (in the US) if** someone is confused, can't be woken, is vomiting while drowsy or passed out, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. Never leave a very drunk person alone to "sleep it off." Anyone who is pregnant, takes prescription medicine, or has liver, kidney, or heart conditions should check with a doctor or pharmacist before using the painkillers or supplements in a kit.

## Why a Bachelorette Weekend Needs Its Own Kind of Hangover Kit

A regular hangover kit assumes one night out and one morning after. A bachelorette or bachelor weekend breaks that assumption in a few ways.

**The drinking is stacked.** A typical weekend runs Friday dinner and drinks, a Saturday brunch with mimosas, a Saturday night out, and sometimes a Sunday send-off. That's several drinking sessions with short gaps in between, and the gaps are filled with late nights and early starts. Hangovers tend to feel worse when you start the next session already short on sleep and fluids, so the kit needs to support recovery across the whole weekend, not just Sunday morning.

**Sleep is the weak point.** Shared rooms, air mattresses, a sofa bed, someone's alarm going off at 7 a.m., a group text at 2 a.m. Alcohol already disrupts sleep. It can help you drift off faster but tends to fragment the second half of the night. Add a noisy rental and you get the classic party-weekend fog that people blame entirely on the drinks. A good kit takes sleep seriously.

**The group is mixed.** The bride's college friends, her sister, her future sister-in-law, a coworker, maybe a pregnant friend, maybe someone who doesn't drink. Some take antidepressants, some take blood pressure pills, some are on birth control and nothing else. You can't build one "medicine bag" that's right for everyone, which is why the safest kits keep medication labeled, single-serve, and optional.

**Travel adds dehydration.** Many of these weekends are destination trips: Nashville, Las Vegas, Scottsdale, a beach town, a lake house. Flights, heat, sun, and walking all add to fluid loss before anyone opens a bottle. A pool day or boat day stacks heat and sun on top of the drinks, which is why sunscreen and extra water belong in the kit, not just the morning-after items.

**It's also a gift.** A bachelorette kit is part welcome bag, part party favor. That's fine, as long as the cute stuff doesn't crowd out the useful stuff.

## The Core Bachelorette Hangover Kit Checklist

Here is the list that does the real work. Everything in this section is cheap, widely available, and safe for almost everyone.

### 1. Water, and a way to keep drinking it

- **A refillable water bottle per person.** This is the single most useful item in the kit. Personalized bottles double as a favor, and a bottle people actually carry gets used far more than a pile of plastic minis.
- **A few bottled waters in the room** for the first night, before anyone finds the grocery store.

Alcohol is a diuretic: it suppresses a hormone (vasopressin) that tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you urinate more than you drink. Dehydration isn't the whole story of a hangover, but it contributes to the headache, dry mouth, and dizziness. A water between drinks and a full glass before bed are the cheapest hangover help there is.

### 2. Electrolyte packets

- **Two to four packets per person** for a weekend, or a box at the shared station.
- Pick a mix of flavors, since tastes vary and a flavor you hate at 9 a.m. won't get drunk.

Electrolyte drinks put back some of the sodium and potassium you lose when you urinate a lot, sweat in the sun, or vomit. They aren't a hangover cure, and for many people plain water plus a salty breakfast does the same job. They're still worth packing because they make people drink more fluid. If you're choosing between brands, our [electrolyte drinks for hangovers comparison](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) breaks down sodium and sugar levels so you can match them to your group.

### 3. Something to eat

- **Salty snacks** like pretzels, crackers, or popcorn for late at night.
- **A gentle breakfast item** like an instant oatmeal cup, a granola bar, or a banana chip pack for the morning.
- **Ginger chews or peppermints** for a queasy stomach.

Food matters twice. Eating before and during drinking slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream, which helps keep the night from getting away from people. Our guide on [what to eat before drinking alcohol](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) goes deeper on this. And the morning after, bland carbohydrates and a bit of salt help settle the stomach and steady blood sugar. Ginger has some evidence for easing nausea in other settings, such as pregnancy and motion sickness, and it's a reasonable, low-risk thing to have on hand.

### 4. Sleep and comfort

- **A sleep mask and foam earplugs.** Arguably the most underrated items on the list for a shared rental.
- **Lip balm** (alcohol plus air conditioning plus sun is hard on lips).
- **Under-eye patches or a face mist**, if your group likes them. These are comfort and fun, not medicine.
- **Hair ties, bobby pins, and makeup wipes.** Purely practical, and someone always needs them.

### 5. Morning headache relief (labeled, optional, single-serve)

- **Single-serve packets of ibuprofen** (or naproxen) are the usual choice for a hangover headache.
- **Attach a small note** that says: "Take with food and water. Skip if you have stomach ulcers, kidney problems, take blood thinners, or are pregnant. Check with a pharmacist if you take prescription meds."

This is the one item in the kit that deserves real care, so it gets its own section below.

### 6. Sun protection for daytime events

- **Travel sunscreen** and maybe a cheap hat for pool, boat, or beach days.

Sunburn and heat stack on top of a hangover. If your itinerary includes a boat day or pool party, this belongs in the kit as much as the electrolytes.

## Painkillers in a Group Kit: The Rules That Keep Everyone Safe

Painkillers are the item most likely to cause real harm in a party kit, mostly through confusion rather than the drugs themselves. Here's what to know.

**Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin** (called NSAIDs, the anti-inflammatory family) are generally the better choice for a hangover headache in healthy adults, because they're processed differently from acetaminophen and don't put the same strain on the liver. Their downside is the stomach. Alcohol already irritates the stomach lining, and NSAIDs add to that. The US drug labels warn people who have three or more drinks a day about the risk of stomach bleeding. So the rule for a kit is: take it in the morning, with food and water, at the label dose, and not repeatedly through the weekend. Our article on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) explains the stomach and kidney risks in more detail.

**Acetaminophen (Tylenol)** is easier on the stomach but harder on the liver when combined with heavy drinking. The liver turns a small part of each dose into a toxic by-product, and heavy drinking makes that by-product easier to build up. One normal dose the morning after a few drinks is unlikely to hurt a healthy person, but taking it while still drinking, or stacking it on top of cold and flu products that also contain acetaminophen, is how people get into trouble. If you include it, label it clearly and keep it separate from the ibuprofen. Read our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) before you decide.

**A few kit rules that prevent most problems:**

1. **Single-serve, labeled packets only.** No loose pills in a pretty jar. Nobody should have to guess what a white tablet is at 8 a.m.
2. **One painkiller type per packet,** with the name and dose on it.
3. **A note telling people to take it with food,** not before or during drinking.
4. **Never "pre-dose" a painkiller before going out.** It doesn't prevent a hangover and it adds strain while your body is busy processing alcohol.
5. **Don't share prescription medication.** Not sleep aids, not anxiety pills, not anything. Many prescription drugs interact badly with alcohol, and you don't know what else your friend has taken.
6. **Skip sleep aids entirely.** Antihistamine sleep aids (the "PM" products) and alcohol are both sedating, and the combination can be more than people expect. Earplugs and a sleep mask are the safer sleep kit.

## Per-Person Bags vs a Shared Recovery Station

There are two ways to set this up, and many groups use both.

### Per-person bags

**Best for:** welcome bags at check-in, groups that are spread across several rooms or hotels, and anyone who wants a keepsake.

Put the non-medicine basics in each bag: water bottle, two electrolyte packets, a snack, ginger chews, lip balm, a sleep mask, earplugs, and hair ties. If you add a painkiller, use a single labeled packet with the note described above.

**Pros:** everyone has what they need in their own room at 3 a.m., and the bags feel personal.
**Cons:** more packing work, more waste, and you're guessing at what each person will use.

### A shared recovery station

**Best for:** a single rental house or suite where everyone shares a kitchen.

Set up one table or counter with a jug or case of water, a box of electrolyte packets, a bowl of salty snacks, breakfast items, a bag of ginger chews, a box of single-serve ibuprofen with the label visible, and sunscreen. Add a small sign with the basics: drink water, eat something, take painkillers with food.

**Pros:** cheaper per person, less waste, easy to restock, and medication stays in its original labeled packaging.
**Cons:** someone has to run to the store on day two, and a station in the kitchen doesn't help the friend stuck in the bathroom upstairs.

**The hybrid that works well:** small per-person bags with the non-medicine essentials, plus a shared station for food, extra electrolytes, and any painkillers or supplements. It keeps medicine visible and labeled, and it keeps the cute part of the gift.

## How to Pace the Kit Across a Multi-Day Weekend

Because a bachelorette weekend is several drinking sessions in a row, it helps to think of the kit as a plan rather than a bag.

**Friday (arrival night).** Travel dehydrates people before the first drink. Hand out water bottles at check-in and encourage everyone to drink one before dinner. Have a real meal before the bars, not just appetizers. Leave a glass of water and an electrolyte packet on each nightstand.

**Saturday morning.** This is the morning that sets up the rest of the weekend. A salty breakfast, water or an electrolyte drink, and an honest look at the day's schedule. If someone feels terrible, the best move is a slow morning, not "hair of the dog." Drinking again to ease a hangover only delays the recovery and adds to the total load.

**Saturday brunch or daytime event.** Mimosas and pool-party drinks go down fast, especially with sun and heat. Alternate each drink with water, eat during the event, and keep sunscreen and water bottles in the beach or pool bag. Bubbly drinks can feel like they hit faster, a point we cover in our [champagne hangover guide](/never-hungover/champagne-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide).

**Saturday night.** The big night, usually after the least sleep. A real dinner beforehand, a water between drinks, and an agreed plan for getting everyone home together. Our [party drinking tips](/never-hungover/party-drinking-tips) cover pacing strategies that don't feel like a lecture.

**Sunday (travel home).** This is the morning the kit matters most. Water, electrolytes, food, and sunglasses for the airport. If anyone is driving home, they need enough time for the alcohol to clear. A morning-after "I feel fine" is not the same as being sober, and coffee or a cold shower doesn't speed that up.

## The Bachelor Party Hangover Kit: What Changes

A bachelor party kit is built on the same core: water, electrolytes, salty food, sleep, and labeled painkillers. The difference is mostly in packaging and the kind of activities involved.

**Common swaps and additions:**

- **Swap the beauty items** (makeup wipes, under-eye patches) for practical ones: a travel toothbrush, deodorant wipes, a phone charging cable, and antacid tablets.
- **Beef jerky or nuts** instead of granola bars, if that's more your group's taste.
- **A stainless steel or insulated bottle** in place of a personalized tumbler.
- **Sunscreen and a hat** if the weekend includes golf, a boat, or a pool day.
- **Antacids** can help with alcohol-related heartburn, though people on other medications should check labels.

**Bachelor-weekend activities that change the kit:**

- **Golf or other outdoor days.** Heat and sun make dehydration worse. Pack extra electrolytes and plan water at every hole, not just at the turn.
- **Steak dinners and late nights.** Heavy, fatty meals before drinking slow absorption, which helps, but rich food plus a lot of alcohol is also a heartburn setup.
- **Boat days.** Sun, heat, and drinking on water make falls and overboard accidents a real risk. Keep a sober captain and a sober person watching the group.
- **Casino nights.** Many casinos keep drinks flowing and have few clocks. Agree on a stop time or a drink count before you start.

The safety rules don't change: no sharing prescription pills, no sleep aids with alcohol, painkillers labeled and taken with food, and someone keeping an eye on the group.

## Destination-Specific Additions

Where you're going changes what's worth packing.

**Las Vegas and desert destinations (Scottsdale, Palm Springs).** Dry desert air, daytime heat, pool parties, and long walks between venues. Double the electrolytes, add sunscreen and a hat, and pack a refillable bottle that stays cold. Air conditioning in hotel rooms is also very drying, so lip balm and a saline nasal spray can make mornings more comfortable.

**Nashville and city-bar weekends.** Lots of walking, crowded bars, and live music until late. Comfortable shoes, foam earplugs (also useful at the venues), and blister bandages earn their place. Pedal taverns and party buses often run in daytime heat, so carry water.

**Beach and lake trips.** Sun is the big multiplier. Reef-safe sunscreen, aloe gel, a hat, and plenty of water. Swimming after drinking is a real drowning risk, so set a rule that nobody swims alone or after heavy drinking.

**Cabins and mountain towns.** At higher altitudes, some people feel alcohol more and wake up with worse headaches, and the dry air dehydrates you faster. Extra water and a slower pace on the first night help.

**Cruises.** All-inclusive drink packages and sun decks make this its own category. See our [drinking on a cruise](/never-hungover/drinking-on-a-cruise) guide.

## What to Leave Out of a Bachelorette Hangover Kit

Some popular kit items are a waste of money, and a few are a bad idea.

- **"Hangover cure" shots and energy drinks.** Caffeine can make you feel more alert, but mixing energy drinks with alcohol can mask how drunk you are, which can lead to drinking more. Coffee the next morning is fine for most people. Energy drinks during the night are a poor choice.
- **Loose pills or unlabeled medication of any kind.** For the reasons covered above.
- **Sleep aids, PM painkillers, or anything with diphenhydramine or doxylamine.** These add sedation on top of alcohol.
- **Prescription anything.** Even if it's "just to help people sleep."
- **"Detox" teas with laxatives.** Diarrhea plus alcohol plus heat is a dehydration recipe.
- **Mini liquor bottles in the hangover kit itself.** Lots of welcome bags include them. That's a separate gift, and it sends a mixed message in a recovery kit. "Hair of the dog" doesn't help a hangover; it just pushes it later.
- **Products that promise to "eliminate" hangovers.** No supplement or drink does that. If the packaging makes that claim, treat it as marketing.

## Budget Tiers: Building a Kit for Any Group

Prices vary a lot by store and region, so think in terms of tiers rather than exact numbers.

**Simple tier (the essentials).** A plain water bottle, two electrolyte packets, a snack bag, ginger chews, earplugs, and lip balm in a small pouch or tote. Most of this can be bought in bulk at a warehouse store or online, which keeps the per-person cost low.

**Mid tier (the welcome bag).** Everything in the simple tier, plus a personalized tumbler or bottle, a sleep mask, makeup wipes or a travel toiletry item, a gentle breakfast item, and sunscreen. This is what most groups are after: useful and a bit special.

**Deluxe tier (the splurge).** Everything above, plus nicer skincare, a silk sleep mask, a custom tote, and an optional supplement at the shared station. Spend the extra on things people will actually use, like a quality water bottle, rather than novelty items that get thrown away.

**A note on splitting costs.** If the group is splitting the bill, keep the medicine and supplements at a shared station rather than buying them for everyone. Not everyone will want them, and it avoids buying a dozen bottles of something three people will use.

## Where DHM Fits In (Honestly)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree (Hovenia dulcis) that shows up in a lot of hangover supplements. Here's what's actually known.

- **The research is early.** The best-known work, from researchers at UCLA and published in the Journal of Neuroscience in 2012, studied DHM in rats and found it reduced signs of intoxication and withdrawal. Other lab and animal research suggests it may support the liver's processing of alcohol. Good human trials are limited.
- **It's not a cure.** There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in everyone or makes heavy drinking safe. It's one optional piece, after water, food, sleep, and pacing.
- **Some people find it helpful.** Many users take it with their last drink or before bed. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers typical amounts and timing.
- **It's not for everyone.** Anyone who is pregnant, breastfeeding, or taking prescription medication should check with a pharmacist or doctor first, as with any supplement.

**How to include it in a group kit.** The cleanest way is one bottle at the shared station with the label visible, rather than splitting capsules into little bags. For a group, a plain DHM product like [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) works well, since it's simple DHM with a clear label and enough servings to cover several people over a weekend. If you prefer a single-serve or combination product, [Flyby Recovery](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0CCK34H46?tag=dhmguide-20) is a lower-cost option that combines DHM with other ingredients. Whatever you choose, put a note beside it: "Optional. Check with a pharmacist if you take prescription meds or are pregnant."

For a broader look at kit tiers beyond party weekends, see our full [hangover kit ideas](/never-hungover/hangover-kit-ideas) guide. Our honest review of [what to take before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-take-before-drinking) covers which pre-drinking supplements have any evidence, and if the weekend leads up to the wedding itself, see [how not to get drunk at a wedding](/never-hungover/how-not-to-get-drunk-at-a-wedding).

## Safety Basics Every Maid of Honor and Best Man Should Know

The person organizing the weekend often ends up as the unofficial safety lead. A few simple habits go a long way.

**Have a sober or low-key buddy each night.** It doesn't have to be the same person, and it doesn't have to be dull. One person drinking less makes it far easier to get everyone home, keep track of phones and bags, and spot trouble.

**Plan rides before anyone drinks.** Book the party bus, share a rideshare plan, or pick the hotel within walking distance. Decide in daylight, not at 1 a.m.

**Keep the group together.** No one gets left at a bar or walks home alone. Agree on a meeting spot and a group chat check-in.

**Watch drinks.** Keep drinks in hand, accept drinks only from the bartender, and leave if anyone suddenly seems far more drunk than they should be based on what they've had. Sudden confusion, extreme drowsiness, or loss of coordination after only a drink or two needs medical attention.

**Make non-drinking easy.** Have mocktails, sparkling water, and good non-alcoholic options at every event. Pregnant guests, people who are taking medication, people who are driving, and people who just don't want to drink should never feel singled out.

**Know the signs of alcohol poisoning.** A hangover is uncomfortable. Alcohol poisoning is an emergency. Call 911 if someone:

- is confused, or can't be woken up
- is vomiting while drowsy or passed out
- has slow breathing (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute) or long pauses between breaths
- has a seizure
- has pale, bluish, cold, or clammy skin
- has a very low body temperature

While you wait for help, keep the person on their side so they don't choke if they vomit, stay with them, and don't give them coffee or a cold shower. Our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) covers what to do step by step. Calling for help is always the right move. Many US states have Good Samaritan laws that offer some protection to people who call for help in an alcohol emergency.

> **When to see a doctor the morning after.** Most party-weekend hangovers fade within a day. Get medical help if someone has vomiting that won't stop or can't keep water down for several hours, vomit with blood or that looks like coffee grounds, severe stomach pain, a severe or unusual headache, chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle, confusion, or fainting. Shaking, sweating, and anxiety that get worse rather than better after heavy drinking for several days in a row can be a sign of alcohol withdrawal, which needs medical care, so say so plainly and get them seen.

## A Simple Bachelorette Hangover Kit Packing List

Copy this into your planning doc.

**Per-person bag:**
- Refillable water bottle
- 2 to 4 electrolyte packets
- Salty snack and a gentle breakfast item
- Ginger chews or peppermints
- Lip balm
- Sleep mask and foam earplugs
- Hair ties and makeup wipes (bachelorette) or deodorant wipes and toothbrush (bachelor)
- Travel sunscreen

**Shared recovery station:**
- Case of water
- Extra electrolyte packets in mixed flavors
- Bread, crackers, bananas, oatmeal cups, or other bland breakfast food
- Single-serve ibuprofen, labeled, with a "take with food" note
- Antacids
- Optional DHM supplement, labeled, with a "check with a pharmacist" note
- A small sign: drink water, eat first, call 911 if someone can't be woken

**Leave out:**
- Loose or unlabeled pills
- Sleep aids and PM products
- Prescription medication of any kind
- Energy drinks for mixing
- Laxative "detox" teas

The kit won't make a big weekend consequence-free, but it will make the mornings easier, keep everyone a bit safer, and let the group actually enjoy the brunch they booked.

faq.question: What should go in a bachelorette hangover kit?
faq.answer: The useful core is a refillable water bottle, a few electrolyte packets, a salty snack, a gentle breakfast item, ginger chews or mints, lip balm, a sleep mask, and earplugs. If you add a painkiller, use single-serve labeled ibuprofen with a note to take it with food. Cute extras like tumblers and face masks are fine, but they shouldn't replace the basics.

faq.question: What goes in a bachelor party hangover kit?
faq.answer: The same core as a bachelorette kit: water, electrolytes, salty food, sleep gear, and labeled single-serve painkillers. Common swaps are deodorant wipes, a travel toothbrush, a charging cable, antacids, and jerky or nuts in place of beauty items. Add sunscreen and a hat for golf, boat, or pool days.

faq.question: Should I put painkillers in a group hangover kit?
faq.answer: You can, with care. Use single-serve, clearly labeled packets only, never loose pills. Ibuprofen is the usual choice for healthy adults, taken in the morning with food and water. Add a note telling people to skip it if they have stomach ulcers, kidney problems, take blood thinners, or are pregnant, and to check with a pharmacist if they take prescription medicine. Keep acetaminophen (Tylenol) separate and clearly labeled because of its liver risk with heavy drinking.

faq.question: Is it safe to share sleep aids or prescription pills on a bachelorette trip?
faq.answer: No. Many prescription medicines and over-the-counter sleep aids interact with alcohol, often by adding sedation, and you don't know what else a friend has taken. Leave sleep aids and PM products out of the kit entirely. Earplugs and a sleep mask are the safer way to help a group sleep in a shared rental.

faq.question: How do you avoid a hangover on a multi-day bachelorette weekend?
faq.answer: Eat a real meal before each drinking session, alternate alcoholic drinks with water, drink a full glass of water before bed, and protect your sleep with earplugs and a mask. Avoid drinking again to ease a hangover, since that only delays recovery. Pace yourself on the big night, which usually comes after the least sleep.

faq.question: Does DHM belong in a bachelorette hangover kit?
faq.answer: It's an optional extra, not a core item. Research on DHM is early and mostly from animal studies, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers for everyone. If you include it, keep one labeled bottle at a shared station with a note to check with a pharmacist if someone is pregnant or takes prescription medicine.

faq.question: When is a party-weekend hangover actually an emergency?
faq.answer: Call 911 if someone is confused or can't be woken, vomits while drowsy or passed out, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale, or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a hangover. Keep the person on their side and stay with them until help arrives.
